title: §.XII strict close: Proof — Frederick Palatine Naumburg 1561 / Augsburg 1566; Philip of Hesse favoring Reformed
pass_a_gloss: For that those no less than these have always been held Associates of the Augsburg Confession is established (1.) by the example of FREDERICK THE PALATINE in the Naumburg Convention in the Year 1561 and at the Augsburg Diet in the Year 1566; on which matter more fully the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung in the Appendix from p. 36 to 43; Pareus in the Iren. pp. 292 and 297; Joh. Crocius in the German tract titled Summarische Nachricht und beweißliche Anzeig: That the Estates and Churches in the German land attached to the Reformed Religion, as fellow-members of the Augsburg Confession, are capable of the Religious Peace — from num. 123 to 130, from p. 54 to 58; likewise in the Comment on the Society of the Augsburg Confession, Question 2, Cap. XVIII and Cap. XXI; and also our Dn. D. Becmann l. c. p. 99 and following. (2.) by the example of PHILIP, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE, constantly favoring the parties of those, i.e. of the Reformed, and with great zeal soliciting and inducing the more rigid, by voice alike and by many written Letters, into the same parties — in Chytraeus in the Acts with the Zwinglians, History from p. 633 and following, and in Calixtus On the Tolerance of the Reformed n. 62 Batavian, and n. 65 of the newest Helmstedt Edition; also in the History of the A. C. of three Theologians written in German and translated into Latin by Chemnitz's son-in-law.
pass_b_english: That the Reformed no less than the Lutherans have always been held Augsburg Confession associates appears (1) from Frederick the Palatine at Naumburg in 1561 and at the Augsburg Diet in 1566.

See more fully the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung, Appendix pp. 36–43; Pareus, Irenicum, pp. 292 and 297; Crocius's German Summarische Nachricht… (nos. 123–130; pp. 54–58), and his Comment on Augsburg Confession Society, Q.2, caps. XVIII and XXI; also our Becmann, loc. cit., p. 99ff.

(2) From Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, who steadily favored the Reformed side and with great zeal pressed the more rigid into it by speech and many letters — in Chytraeus's Acts with the Zwinglians from p. 633ff.; Calixtus, On Tolerance of the Reformed, n. 62 (Batavian) and n. 65 (newest Helmstedt); and the History of the A.C. by three theologians, written in German and Latinized by Chemnitz's son-in-law.
source_text: Nam istos non minus, atque hos, August. Confess. Socios habitos semper fuisse (1.) exemplo FRIDERICI PALATINI in Conventu Naumburgico Anno 1561. & Comitiis Augustanis Anno 1566. constat; qua de re prolixius Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung in Append. a p. 36. ad 43. Pareus in Iren. p. m. 292. & 297. Joh. Crocius in tractatu Germanico nuncupato: Summarische Nachricht und beweißliche Anzeig: Daß die im deutschen Land der Reformirten Religion zugethane Stände und Kirchen/als Mitgenossen der Augspurgischen Confession, des Religions-Friedens fähig seyn/ à num. 123. ad 130. à pag. 54. ad 58. itemque in Comment. de August. Confess. Societate, Questione 2. Cap. XVIII. & Cap. XXI. nec non Dn. D. Becmannus noster l. c. pag. 99. & seqq. (2.) exemplo PHILIPPI, HASSIAE LANDGRAVII, istorum, i.e. Reformatorum partibus constanter faventis, & rigidiores, voce pariter ac scriptis Literis plurimis, in easdem partes, magno cum zelo sollicitantis ac inducentis, apud Chytraeum in Actis cum Zwinglianis, Histor. à pag. 633. & seqq. & apud Calixtum de Tolerantia Reformatorum n. 62. Batavica, & n. 65. novissima Helmst. Edit. nec non in Historia A. C. trium Theologorum germanicè conscripta & a Chemnitii genero in Lat. translata.
